• Updates are a BACK DOOR to your computer. Microsoft can install whatever they want on there when you let them do that. As can anyone who has an auto-update procedure. And they have used this badly in the past. Force installs with Windows 10. The fact that an uninstalled Windows 10 system is never going to be quite right again, especially with the arbitrary auto-delete of uninstallation data. Plus the fact that it basically held your data hostage once it had automatically installed, especially since, towards the end, Microsoft was using deception to get people to "agree." That's what you get for updating your software - betrayal and infiltration.

  • Updates CHANGE THINGS. These aren't just tweaking a few instructions to eliminate a logic error that allows arbitrary code to be injected somewhere. Do you like your OS the way it is? Well, with Windows 10, it isn't staying the way it is. Microsoft is radically altering the interface piece by piece, and you get no say in it except maybe being able to delay it. Consider how hostile they were with forcing changes down your throat with Windows 10. Unless something is done - and it probably won't be - they'll ramp that shit up as fast as they can. As-is, Windows 10's update system already sometimes kills software that it doesn't like, without asking the user.

  • Updates give CONTROL of your system away. "But you'll give it away to the hackers if you don't, herp derp," Well, that's gonna happen no matter what you do if your machine is badly configured, updates aren't a panacea by any means. Ever have your machine decide to reboot without your authorization in the middle of the night? It isn't pretty when you're working on things. The fact that "you should have saved" is no excuse for the machine deliberately taking control away from the user, unless you want the company to be your nanny. Heck, with current things, they try to prevent you from being able to turn off updates at all. And what about all those smart phone patches that are designed explicitly to take away your ability to root the phone? If you don't have an auto-root switch of some kind (which is TOTALLY possible, they just need to have it be a hardware switch or two), then those patches are taking away your ability to actually control the phone. If you don't have root, then in general, that computer is someone else's. Not only that, at least with the hackers I know I have some defense against them. If my OS has a back door custom built for an entity that I cannot trust, that's worse - I'm already hacked down to the deepest level. And they intend to keep it that way. Do companies have the right to dictate what you can do with that computer of yours? I certainly don't think so, and if you do, you should think more about the implications of companies having final say over the devices that surround you.

  • Updates BREAK THINGS. I've run an update on a brand new, day-out-of-the-box, brand-name computer and the result was so bad that I almost returned the machine. Windows 10's force-installs are another issue along these lines and I shudder to imagine what might happen with a new machine that might burp at that. Plus some are DESIGNED to break things, such as a lovely driver update that actually physically screwed up chips that a company decided were counterfeit (see: FTDI, maker of serial interface chips). Your machine may have been broken because of this, because some company said it should be. This is even worse when you consider the "break things" angle. And what about software that you may love and use every day? Are you prepared for the day that you get an update that says you can't use it anymore? They're working on breaking backwards compatibility right now (Intel's stuff about killing legacy BIOS comes to mind). "Oh you should upgrade lol." Who is anyone to say what I can and can't do with my machine? I'm not dumping that software on anyone else's desk. Some old software has some very well known users, such as William F. Buckley and George R. R. Martin. That also doesn't help companies that can't afford to update their stuff every time Microsoft dictates that they should.

  • Updates make you RELIANT on the company for your machine. Do you relish the idea of software that dies because the company says it dies? That kind of software is already out there, so it's hardly a technological leap. They're just trying to push it onto your desktop now. They already do it psychologically. Listen to all of the people even in this thread who say, "Windows 7 is gonna go away in 2020!" No, it isn't. Windows 7 will still function in 2021, and 2022, and so on, so long as hardware continues to support it. But the companies want you to think that they, forevermore, shall dictate what software you can and cannot use on your machine. Some people encourage this even - I've read columns by security "experts" that insist that XP should have a kill switch embedded by Microsoft, allowing them to prevent it from ever booting again, after it was no longer supported. They're working up to making this enforceable on hardware and making hardware hacking illegal (DMCA gives them a legal argument already), which means they will own the machine you paid for. They will own all the machines, period, if they get their way.

Updates are not a panacea. They are a band-aid that costs your soul, and a simple "magic wand" for security "experts" to wave about. They are part of a major series of steps with the end goal of making sure that you will never own a computer again, you will pay for a computer that is unwaveringly loyal to a corporation or a government. The tragedy is that nobody is going to be listening to any of this until they find the police showing up to their door for downloading a video that their computer snitched on them for. Heck, most people who are implementing these things will likely not even realize it until it's too late - I remember getting bitched at by a developer (or so he claimed to be) that bitched about people having the option to NOT send crash dumps directly to him for debugging. Crash dumps, as in everything you were working on in memory in that program, if not the computer outright. That is deeply invasive on levels I can't even begin to start on.

The privacy and security nightmare that we're looking at did not pop up overnight and it didn't come from nowhere. It came from things like this, things that should be excellent ideas, twisted beyond recognition. One of the roots of this is that large, heavily-invested individuals, companies, organizations, and governments want to make sure that the computer you are using is no longer your computer. It's the same with cloud computing, and that is not so ironically the source of many security disasters with it. They're also pushing that angle with cell phones - have been for a while, in fact.

These organizations and individuals have proven time and again that they cannot be trusted. Updates are a way of making sure you fully re-invest yourself in that trust, on a weekly basis.
